interactions.label: A woman's karyotype report reads 45,XX,rob(14;21). She is clinically healthy. Wh

params.question: A woman's karyotype report reads 45,XX,rob(14;21). She is clinically healthy. Which of the following BEST explains why she has only 45 chromosomes yet is phenotypically normal?

answers.text: She has lost the entire short arm of chromosome 21, but this region carries no essential genes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes carry mainly repetitive DNA, the correct explanation is that the long arms — which contain the essential genes — are preserved in the fused chromosome.

answers.text: The long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21 have fused into one chromosome, preserving all essential genetic material

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In a Robertsonian translocation, the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at their centromeres. The total count drops to 45, but virtually all essential genetic material is retained, so the carrier is phenotypically normal.

answers.text: Non-disjunction during meiosis removed one chromosome entirely, which was compensated by gene duplication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-disjunction produces cells with an extra or missing chromosome (aneuploidy). A Robertsonian translocation is a structural rearrangement — a fusion of two chromosomes — not a segregation error.

answers.text: Her karyotype is abnormal and she will inevitably develop Down syndrome later in life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A balanced translocation carrier has the normal gene dosage and will not develop Down syndrome. However, she is at increased risk of producing gametes with an unbalanced arrangement, which could lead to trisomy 21 in her offspring.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a Robertsonian translocation, two acrocentric chromosomes (such as 14 and 21) fuse at their centromeres into a single large chromosome. The count drops to 45, but no essential genes are lost, so the carrier is phenotypically normal — though at risk of passing an unbalanced form to offspring.

Well done. A balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier is phenotypically normal because the essential genetic material from both chromosomes is preserved in the fused chromosome, even though the total count is 45.

interactions.label: Turner syndrome should only be suspected when a girl presents with the full clas

params.question: Turner syndrome should only be suspected when a girl presents with the full classic triad of short stature, webbed neck, and primary amenorrhoea.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. In mosaic Turner syndrome, only some cells carry the monosomy, so the phenotype can be very subtle — sometimes only short stature with no webbing, no amenorrhoea, and no other classic features. Waiting for the full triad would delay diagnosis and miss the window for timely growth hormone therapy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Mosaic Turner syndrome (45,X/46,XX) can present with isolated short stature and no other dysmorphic features. Any girl with unexplained short stature warrants karyotyping, because catching Turner syndrome early allows timely growth hormone therapy.

params.question: Nearly half of all children with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease, most commonly an atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD). Which of the following BEST explains this high prevalence?

answers.text: Atlantoaxial instability in Down syndrome compresses the great vessels during foetal development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Atlantoaxial instability affects the cervical spine and spinal cord, not the heart. Both are complications of trisomy 21, but through entirely different mechanisms — ligamentous laxity for the spine versus disrupted endocardial cushion formation for the heart.

answers.text: The extra copy of chromosome 21 produces a gene-dosage effect that disrupts endocardial cushion formation during embryogenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Overexpression of genes on the extra chromosome 21 disrupts the development of endocardial cushions, which normally fuse to form the atrial and ventricular septa. This is why AVSD is the hallmark cardiac defect in Down syndrome.

answers.text: Advanced maternal age independently causes cardiac malformations regardless of the chromosomal status of the foetus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Advanced maternal age increases the risk of non-disjunction (and hence trisomy 21), but the cardiac defects result from the extra chromosome's effect on endocardial cushion development, not from maternal age directly.

answers.text: Congenital heart disease in Down syndrome is coincidental, occurring at the same rate as in the general population

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Congenital heart disease occurs in roughly 40–50% of children with Down syndrome, compared with less than 1% in the general population. This marked difference confirms a direct causal link to trisomy 21.

overallFeedback.feedback: The extra copy of chromosome 21 overexpresses genes involved in endocardial cushion formation, disrupting cardiac septation during embryogenesis. This gene-dosage mechanism explains why nearly half of all children with Down syndrome are born with heart defects, most commonly AVSD.

Exactly. The gene-dosage effect from the extra chromosome 21 disrupts endocardial cushion development, making AVSD the most common cardiac defect in Down syndrome — and the reason echocardiography is mandatory in every newborn with the diagnosis.

params.question: Parents of a 3-month-old infant with Down syndrome, whose cardiac evaluation is reassuring, ask when developmental support should begin. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice?

answers.text: Begin a structured early intervention programme now, including physiotherapy for hypotonia and speech therapy for language development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Evidence shows that early intervention started in infancy — physiotherapy, speech therapy, and developmental stimulation — produces significantly better cognitive and social outcomes than intervention delayed until school age.

answers.text: Wait until the child is 2 years old so that developmental delays can be clearly documented before starting therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting to document delays misses the critical early developmental window. Intervention should be proactive, not reactive — the goal is to optimise development from the start, not to wait for deficits to accumulate.

answers.text: Refer the child to a residential institution where specialists can provide round-the-clock care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modern management of Down syndrome aims for active inclusion and supported independence within the family and community, not institutional segregation. Outcomes are far better with family-based early intervention.

answers.text: Developmental support is unnecessary because intellectual disability in Down syndrome is fixed and cannot be improved

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While intellectual disability is a feature of Down syndrome, its severity is not fixed. Early intervention, inclusive education, and proactive multidisciplinary support have been shown to significantly improve functional outcomes across all developmental domains.

overallFeedback.feedback: Early intervention should begin in infancy, not wait for documented delays. A structured programme of physiotherapy, speech therapy, and developmental stimulation, coordinated by the paediatrician across multiple disciplines, gives the best cognitive and social outcomes.

Well done. The paediatrician should initiate early intervention immediately — a structured, evidence-based programme coordinated across physiotherapy, speech therapy, and other disciplines to optimise the child's developmental trajectory.

params.question: A couple receive a cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening result showing high risk for trisomy 21 at 12 weeks of gestation. They ask whether their baby definitely has Down syndrome. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate response?

answers.text: Yes — cfDNA is highly accurate, so this result confirms the diagnosis and you should begin planning for a child with Down syndrome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Despite its high sensitivity, cfDNA remains a screening test that estimates probability. Presenting it as a confirmed diagnosis is a serious counselling error that could lead to irreversible decisions based on incomplete information.

answers.text: No — cfDNA is a screening test; a diagnostic procedure such as amniocentesis is needed to confirm trisomy 21 through karyotyping

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. cfDNA screens for risk but cannot provide a karyotype. Amniocentesis or CVS yields a definitive karyotype, which also reveals whether the trisomy is free, translocation, or mosaic — each carrying a different recurrence risk for future pregnancies.

answers.text: No — cfDNA results are unreliable and should be disregarded entirely in favour of ultrasound alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: cfDNA has very high sensitivity and specificity for trisomy 21 and is a valuable screening tool. Dismissing it entirely would be inappropriate — a high-risk result must be followed up with a confirmatory diagnostic procedure.

answers.text: Yes — but only if the mother is over 35 years of age, since cfDNA is unreliable in younger women

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: cfDNA performance is not limited to women over 35. Regardless of maternal age, however, it remains a screening test — a high-risk result always requires confirmatory karyotyping before a definitive diagnosis is communicated.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cell-free DNA is a powerful screening tool, but it does not replace karyotyping. A definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome requires amniocentesis or CVS, which provides the karyotype and identifies the mechanism — free trisomy 21, Robertsonian translocation, or mosaicism — each carrying different implications for the child and for future pregnancies.

Exactly. The distinction between screening and diagnosis is fundamental to genetic counselling. A high-risk cfDNA result warrants confirmatory karyotyping, which also identifies the trisomy mechanism — free, translocation, or mosaic — guiding both prognosis and recurrence counselling.
